The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered to take action over odours

Milpitas, an affluent city in California's Silicon Valley tech hub, has an odour problem.

For decades, residents have had to endure rank smells wafting from industrial sites, among them a 342-acre landfill.

"When I first moved here, I could not open my window for over 10 years," says Chia-Ling Kong, an engineer for a tech firm who lives around half a mile from the dump.

While things have got better in recent years, Kong says she and her neighbours must still contend with around "two or three hours of bad smells a day".

Perhaps befitting Silicon Valley, the community is putting its hopes in technology.

The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered by local authorities to use drones and install monitors to systematically track and measure the chemicals responsible for bad odours. They have also been told to automate the collection of landfill gases responsible for smells.

Kong is optimistic a data-driven approach will make a difference. "Hopefully with this continuous monitoring, it makes it easier to pinpoint problems at the moment it starts."

The operators of the landfill say they are committed to operating it safely and protecting air quality.

Just like in Milpitas, where Kong is part of a citizen's campaign against the odours, communities around the world are raising a stink about bad smells making day-to-day life miserable. Sometimes a rubbish dump is to blame, or it might be a sewage treatment works, or a reeking factory.

When the complaints start stacking up, resolving them is not always simple. Many countries have no regulations in place dictating how to manage smells.

In the US, for example, the Environmental Protection Agency does not regulate environmental odours as a pollutant. This leaves states and local governments to take charge of the issue.

Urban sprawl is often part of the problem, bringing communities closer to stinky facilities that may historically have been kept at a distance.

This is creating more demand for technologies to monitor and prevent smells. Odour consultant Micheal Bull says people are increasingly concerned about neighbourhood stinks.

"You're getting developments being built nearer to odorous processes… as land has become more valuable, there is also infilling," Bull says. He is speaking about his experiences in the UK, but it's a similar story in many parts of the world.

Bad smells from waste sites are among the most difficult to resolve

The technologies used to tackle industrial pongs generally fall into three categories: they absorb odours; convert them into something less smelly through a chemical reaction; or burn them away.

Experts on fixing industrial odours say that the best technologies, when used correctly, can remove 90% or more of the target compounds responsible for smells.

But this can be expensive and some operators opt for simpler and cheaper solutions. These include masking odours from landfill or sewage processing by spraying giant quantities of deodorisers.

Odour experts contacted for this article were dubious about the effectiveness of such industrial scale air fresheners. "In my view they're not likely to change the odours," says Bull, who likens them to fabric conditioner.

Bad smells from waste sites – a common cause of complaints – are among the stinkiest and most difficult to resolve, according to Carlos Diaz, an environmental consultant based in Spain. "Landfill is difficult to treat because you have a very large surface," he says.

In some places at least, technology is making a real difference. Residents in Des Moines, Iowa, have long complained of the so-called Eastside Funk, a putrid scent that residents report drifts over parts of the city.

A study commissioned by city authorities showed that a trio of industrial meat companies were among culprits.

"Within 10 miles, there's about half a million people," says Dalton Jacobus, who works in the Department of Neighborhood Services. "If the winds are out of the wrong direction, 100,000 people can be in the middle of that odour plume."

The authorities are now paying around $240,000 (£182,000) a year on technology to track the stink, so they can take action. "What we wanted to do was build a ring of odour monitors around the facilities that we suspected of emitting odours," says Jacobus.

The monitors, which measure levels of chemical compounds in the air, work in combination with a weather station to provide real-time data on the concentrations that are coming from each facility based off the wind patterns.

This has put an end to finger pointing about who's to blame each time a smell sparks complaints, says Jacobus. "Now we can say with reasonable certainty that 'this odour event did originate from your facility, what was going on'?"

In Des Moines, authorities have set up "electronic noses" to pinpoint bad smells

Meanwhile, some of the sites that have been blamed for causing unpleasant smells in Des Moines have spent millions of dollars to upgrade their own odour control systems.

Smithfield Foods, which operates a meat processing in Des Moines, says it has invested $2m to install a regenerative thermal oxidiser that destroys the chemicals associated with bad smells. Even so, the company says it does not believe it is the source of odour complaints.

Before installing the monitors – which some local companies help pay for – officials in Des Moines would drive out to the source of a complaint to sniff the air.

Relying on the human nose to sniff out industrial smells is still commonplace. Claudia Barrios Obregón from Kunak, the company behind the monitors in Des Moines, says: "Right now, the way that cities control or measure odours is olfactometry: a human panel measures and gives an opinion of what the odour is like. But that's not that realistic."

The Spanish company's monitors are an example of so-called electronic noses that make it easier to detect smells.

Whatever technology is used, it can be hard to keep everyone happy, as smells are so subjective. "Unfortunately, the general rule is that the nastier we perceive the odour to be, the more sensitive towards it we are," says Johan Lundström, a professor in the science of smell at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden.

Find out how to listen to other BBC stations

World Service , · 17 Oct 2026 , · 39 mins

The first Test between South Africa and Australia was overshadowed by bad light in Durban. Australia won by 214 runs, but the game lost more than 60 overs due to bad light. Should they have used the pink ball to get more play? Alison Mitchell, Jim Maxwell and Sunil Gupta debate if using a pink ball is the best solution. Cricketers are often seen as unbreakable, entertaining us week after week, competing at the highest level and chasing sporting victory. For many, it's a dream career, but for some that is far from reality. Gloucestershire seamer Craig Miles, has decided enough is enough and has retired from the sport at the age of 32, to protect his "mental well-being". He tells Stumped what led to his decision. Plus, England's Ollie Pope has pulled out of the players draft for the inaugural Afghanistan Premier League. Pope was among a number of English players, who entered the draft and have come under criticism, given the Taliban's oppression of women and girls. We examine the ethical questions surrounding involvement in the competition and ask where responsibility lies: with individual players, or with cricket's governing bodies? Photo: Australia leave the field as play is stopped due to bad light during day 2 of the 1st Dafabet Test match between South Africa and Australia at Hollywoodbets Kingsmead Stadium on October 10, 2026 in Durban, South Africa. (Credit: Gallo Images/Getty Images)

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report , and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights , open data , open values , and full training details .

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+ , FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency .

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO) .

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit . We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository , based on lm-evaluation-harness fork .

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models ( blog , code ). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate ( leaderboard , paper ).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals . This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly . Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements , including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report . We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection , including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection . Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom , Infomaniak , Phoeniqs , and other companies listed in our General Availability guide . The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide .

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0 : sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form , and reach out through the options on our Contact page . We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542 .

MN202610_12yaupgswwi.t:
Huye: Umuryango utegamiye kuri Leta wa Rosalie Foundation watangije umushinga ugamije gufasha abanyeshuri bo mu miryango itishoboye kubona ibikoresho by’ishuri n’ibindi byangombwa bikenerwa mu myigire, mu rwego rwo kugabanya ikibazo cy’abana bata ishuri cyangwa bahagarika amasomo kubera kubura ubushobozi.

Uyu mushinga witwa Back-to-School Support Project, watangijwe ku bufatanye n’Akarere ka Huye, watangiriye mu mashuri ane aherereye mu Mirenge ya Huye na Tumba, aho abanyeshuri 80 bahereye bafashwa kubona ibikoresho by’ishuri, imyambaro, inkweto, ibikapu, ibikoresho by’isuku n’amafunguro yo ku ishuri.

Uyu mushinga ugamije gukemura zimwe mu mbogamizi zituma abana bo mu miryango ifite ubushobozi buke badakomeza amashuri uko bikwiye, zirimo kubura ibikoresho by’ishuri, imyambaro, inkweto, amafaranga y’ishuri n’ibindi bibazo bishingiye ku bukene.

Abanyeshuri bafashijwe kubona amakayi, amakaramu, imyambaro y’ishuri, inkweto, ibikapu, ibikoresho by’isuku ndetse n’amafunguro yo ku ishuri.

Uyu mushinga kandi wafashije gushyiraho ibikoresho bikenewe mu byumba byagenewe abakobwa (Girls’ Rooms), kugira ngo bakomeze kwiga badahagaritswe n’ibibazo bijyanye n’isuku n’imibereho yabo.

Abanyeshuri bagiye kungukira kuri iyi gahunda bagaragaje ko kubura ibikoresho n’ibindi byangombwa by’ishuri byagiye bibagiraho ingaruka, bamwe bagasiba ishuri, abandi bagahagarika amasomo by’igihe gito kubera ibibazo by’ubushobozi bw’imiryango yabo.

Umwe muri bo wiga mu mwaka wa gatatu w’amashuri yisumbuye (S3) muri GS Cyarwa, yavuze ko kuba abana na sekuru ugeze mu zabukuru bituma rimwe na rimwe ajya gushaka amafaranga aho kwiga, kugira ngo abone uko babaho.

Yagize ati: “Mbana na sogokuru ugeze mu zabukuru. Hari igihe nasibaga ishuri nkajya gushaka amafaranga ntwaza abantu imizigo no gushaka ibikoresho. Kubura ibikoresho by’ishuri no kutishyura amafaranga y’ishuri byagiraga ingaruka ku myigire yanjye. Ubu bufasha buzatuma nshobora kwibanda ku masomo.”

Undi wiga mu mwaka wa mbere w’amashuri yisumbuye (S1) muri GS Cyarwa, yavuze ko yagiye ahura n’ingorane zo kubura ibikoresho bihagije, bikagira ingaruka ku buryo yiga.

Ati: “Nari mfite inkweto imwe gusa kandi nkandikira amasomo atandukanye mu ikayi imwe. Ibi bikoresho ngiye kubona bizamfasha kwiga neza.”

Mugenzi wabo wiga mu mwaka wa kabiri w’amashuri yisumbuye (S2) muri GS Musange, yavuze ko ibibazo byo mu rugo no kubura ibikoresho by’ishuri byari byaramuteye guhagarika amasomo by’igihe gito, ndetse akegera no kuba yareka ishuri burundu.

Yagize ati: “Nari narahagaritswe ku ishuri, kandi nari ngiye kurireka kubera ibibazo byo mu rugo no kubura ibikoresho. Nakoreraga amasomo atatu mu ikayi imwe, ndetse rimwe na rimwe tukoherezwa mu rugo kubera ibibazo by’amafunguro yo ku ishuri. Ubu hari ubufasha bugiye kuboneka.”

Ubuhamwa bw’aba banyeshuri bugaragaza ko ubukene bwo mu miryango imwe n’imwe ari imbogamizi, mu zituma abana batiga neza, abandi bakajya basiba cyangwa bagahagarika amasomo kubera kubura ibyangombwa by’ibanze bikenerwa ku ishuri.

Binyuze muri uyu mushinga, Rosalie Foundation irateganya kugabanya izo nzitizi, kugira ngo abana bo mu miryango itishoboye babashe gukomeza amasomo yabo badahangayikishijwe no kubura ibikoresho by’ishuri n’ibindi bikenerwa buri munsi.

Gufasha abana kubona amafunguro n’ibikoresho by’isuku na byo biri muri gahunda igamije kuborohereza kwiga neza.

Uwimana Josephine, watangije Rosalie Foundation, wavukiye muri Cyarwa mu Karere ka Huye, yavuze ko uyu mushinga utangiranye n’abana 80, ariko ko gahunda ari ugukomeza gufasha abandi bana bafite ibibazo bisa n’ibyo.

Yagize ati: “Turatangirana n’abana 80, ariko tuzakomeza. Leta ntishobora gukora byose yonyine, natwe tugomba kugira uruhare. Iyo abana batize, bashobora kurangirira mu muhanda cyangwa bakishora mu biyobyabwenge. Tuzafasha buri mwana n’ababyeyi be kugira ngo buri mwana w’Umunyarwanda abashe kwiga. Umuntu wese ubuza umwana kwiga aba amuzitiriye ubuzima bwe bwose.”

Yashimangiye ko intego y’uyu muryango ari ugufatanya n’izindi nzego n’abafatanyabikorwa kugira ngo abana baturuka mu miryango ifite ubushobozi buke batava mu ishuri kubera ibibazo by’ubukene.

Kagabo Joseph, Umujyanama wa Komite Nyobozi y’Akarere ka Huye, yavuze ko ikibazo cy’abana bata amashuri kigihari, nubwo kigenda kigabanuka kubera ubufatanye bw’inzego za Leta n’abafatanyabikorwa batandukanye.

Yagize ati: “Abana bata amashuri baracyahari, ariko umubare wabo uragenda ugabanuka bitewe n’ubufatanye n’abafatanyabikorwa. Turasaba ababyeyi kurera neza abana babo no kubohereza ku ishuri. Abana na bo ndetse n’abayobozi bafite inshingano zo kugira uruhare mu gukemura iki kibazo.”

Yongeyeho ko ubufatanye bw’ababyeyi, inzego z’ibanze n’abafatanyabikorwa ari ingenzi mu gukumira ikibazo cy’abana bata ishuri, kuko kurwanya ubukene bubabuza kwiga bisaba uruhare rwa buri wese.

Rosalie Foundation ni umuryango nyarwanda utegamiye kuri Leta watangijwe muri Mata 2026, ufite icyicaro mu Karere ka Gasabo mu Mujyi wa Kigali.

Umushinga wo gufasha abanyeshuri ni wo wa mbere utangijwe n’uyu muryango, ukaba uteganya gukomeza gukorana n’abafatanyabikorwa kugira ngo ugere no mu tundi turere tw’igihugu.

Uyu mushinga uje ari imwe mu ngamba zo gufasha abana bo mu miryango itishoboye kubona amahirwe yo gukomeza amashuri, aho kubura ibikoresho, imyambaro cyangwa amafunguro bitakomeza kuba impamvu zituma basiba cyangwa bahagarika amasomo.

Biteganyijwe ko gukomeza kwagura iyi gahunda no kongera umubare w’abanyeshuri bafashwa bizagira uruhare mu kugabanya inzitizi zishingiye ku bukene zibangamira uburenganzira bw’abana ku burezi, bityo bakabasha gukomeza kwiga no kwiteza imbere.

MN202610_18l5c7mjjn4.t:
Gatsibo: Umuturage umaranye imyaka myinshi uburwayi bw’ibihaha n’impyiko, ndetse akaba yararwaje abana be indwara “avuga ko zanze gukira”, arasaba abagiraneza kumufasha kubona uko yivuza.

Mageze Esdras atuye mu Murenge wa Gitoki, Akagari ka Bukomane, mu Mudugudu wa Gakiri.

Mu kiganiro n’UMUSEKE, avuga ko uburwayi amaranye imyaka itatu bwizanye ariko ko bwagiye bwiyongera. Ngo basanze arwaye ibihaha, impyiko afite na gaz mu gifu.

Ubuyobozi bw’Akarere ka Gatsibo bwemeye kubafasha kujya kwa muganga mu gihe cya Covid -19 ndetse bubandikira Ibaruwa yo kwivurizaho nk’umuryango utishoboye, ariko ntibahawe ubufasha bwose bakeneye, kuko na n’ubu byabananiye kugera kwa muganga i Kanombe.

Mageza avuga ko ubu aribwa mu mutima, yabuze ubushobozi bwo kujya i Kanombe, we n’abana be kugira ngo bafashwe n’abaganga, kandi ngo afite n’umwe mu Bitaro bya Kiziguro yananiwe kwishyura.

Ibitaro bya Gisirikare i Kanombe, byari byamuhaye ‘transfer’ umujyana ku muganga uvura indwara z’ibihaha, ariko Mageza abura ubushobozi bwo kujyayo.

Yagize ati “ Hari nubwo banyohereje guca mu cyuma cyo mu Bitaro by’Umwami Faisal, ariko mbura ubushobozi kuko bambwiye ngo nitwaze Frw 200,000. Icyo gihe nabwo mbura ubushobozi bwo kujya kwa muganga.”

Mageze avuga ko kubera gutinda kwivuza, yaje kurwara impyiko n’igifu na byo ubu bikaba bihangayikishije ubuzima bwe .

Ati “Igifu cyange basanze kirimo gaz, banyandikiye imiti ngo mpite nyitangira ariko mbura ubushobozi. Ibi bibazo byose byampuriyeho ku buryo n’iyo mbyutse mu gitondo nkaya (kwikokomora) ibintu birimo amaraso.”

Yongeraho ati “Ndasaba abagiraneza ko bantera inkunga nkajya kwa muganga, nkivuza. Ndamutse mbonye abagiraneza, abaganga bakankurikirana nshobora gukira.”

Avuga ko muri ubwo burwayi bwe, n’abana be imibereho imugoye kuko ubu nta kintu abasha gukora, kandi ko akenera ibimutunga adafite ubushobozi.

Umunyamabanga Nshingwabikorwa w’Umurenge wa Gitoki, Furaha Frank, yabwiye UMUSEKE ko ikibazo cy’uyu muturage bakimenye bityo bamusabye kuzana taransiferi (transfer) imwemerera kujya kwivuza ku Bitaro bya Kanombe, ndetse ko biteguye kumufasha.

Ati “ Yarampamagaye ndamubwira ngo azane taransiferi, azane n’ibyangombwa bigaragaza ko nta bushobozi afite biva mu Mudgudu ahabwe uburyo ajya kwa muganga. Twiteguye kumufasha, ariko azanye izo mpapuro kugira ngo tuzagaragaze uko umutungo wa leta wakoreshejwe.”

Gusa Mageze avuga ko kugeza ubu byagorana kubona iyo taransiferi kuko agifite umwenda ku Kigo Nderabuzima cya Kiziguro kandi no kubona amafaranga y’urugendo ajya gushaka izo mpapuro bitamworohera.

Uyu yongeraho ko usibye we, n’abana be barwaye uburwayi avuga ko budakira kuko ariko yabwiwe, umwe yabyimbye mu myanya y’ibanga undi agenda abyimba mu maso.

Ubaye ushaka gufasha Mageza wamubona kuri nimero + (250) 789 895 137, cyangwa +(250) 735 054 738.

Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here .

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp , vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template , enabling add_generation_prompt=True , tokenize=True , return_dict=True , and return_tensors="pt" . Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template .

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch , and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom .

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation ). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t . The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0 , which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map . It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l , like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w) , separated from each other along l . Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity . This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.
